title: On his wise shoulders through the checkerwork of leaves the sun flung spangles, dancing coins.
html_source:
Mr Deasy proves himself quite the hypocrite in his anti-semitism, as he directs Stephen hold tightly his money earlier in the chapter, “Because you don’t save, Mr Deasy said, pointing his finger. You don’t know yet what money is. Money is power. When you have lived as long as I have. I know, I know. If youth but knew. But what does Shakespeare say? Put but money in thy purse.” Later, when asked of the nature of a merchant, or profiteer in general, “A merchant, Stephen said, is one who buys cheap and sells dear, jew or gentile, is he not?” he responds that these specific people are different, “They sinned against the light, Mr Deasy said gravely. And you can see the darkness in their eyes. And that is why they are wanderers on the earth to this day.”

Mr Deasy professes such things as to hold money so closely, as it “is power,” but is prejudiced to the Jews, who are following exactly as he believes, but finds them morally reprehensible—that “they sinned against the light.”

Also, that Mr Deasy’s departure is described with the sun having “flung spangles, dancing coins”, with “coins” specifically described, this further observes his compulsion toward money in general.
